## Deficits and private investment

When the government borrows, does it take saving away from private investment? Here we compare the U.S. budget balance with the private investment rate.

<!-- cell -->

### Fig. 5: U.S. private investment and the budget deficit

**Goal.** Ask whether budget deficits **crowd out** investment, using the saving-investment identity, equation (9).

The data are gross private domestic investment and government saving (the federal budget balance, from the
national accounts), both in percent of GDP, for calendar years.

```{python}
saving = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "fig18-5.csv")
saving.head(3)
```

Equation (9) says that investment minus government saving is the saving of households, firms and
foreigners. Our function `private_and_foreign_saving` computes it, and the chart hides it until you click its
name in the legend. The buttons compare the averages before and after 1980.

```{python}
named_saving = saving.rename(columns={"investment_share": "Investment", "gov_saving_share": "Government saving"})
named_saving["Private + foreign saving"] = private_and_foreign_saving(named_saving.Investment,
                                                                      named_saving["Government saving"])
saving_by_year = named_saving.set_index("year")
SPLITS = {"1960–1979": (1960, 1979), "1980–2025": (1980, 2025)}


def saving_chart(period="1980–2025"):
    """Fig. 18.5: investment and government saving (% of GDP), with their averages over one period."""
    start, end = SPLITS[period]
    I, S = period_mean(saving_by_year.Investment, start, end), period_mean(saving_by_year["Government saving"], start, end)
    fig = px.line(named_saving, x="year", y=["Investment", "Government saving", "Private + foreign saving"],
                  color_discrete_sequence=[BLUE, GREEN, GRAY], range_y=[-15, 35],
                  labels={"year": "Year", "value": "Percentage of GDP", "variable": "Series"},
                  title=f"{period}: investment averaged {I:.1f}%, government saving {S:.1f}% of GDP")
    fig.update_traces(line_width=3)
    fig.update_traces(selector=dict(name="Private + foreign saving"), visible="legendonly", line_dash="dash")
    fig.add_hline(y=0, line=dict(color="black", width=1, dash="dash"))
    add_period_means(fig, saving_by_year, ["Investment", "Government saving"], [BLUE, GREEN], start, end)
    fig.update_xaxes(range=[1959, 2026.5])
    fig.update_layout(legend=dict(x=0.01, y=0.57, xanchor="left", yanchor="top", bgcolor="rgba(255,255,255,0.8)"),
                      legend_title_text="")
    return fig
```

```{python}
#| kind: widget
interact(saving_chart, period=ToggleButtons(options=list(SPLITS), value="1980–2025", description="averages over"));
```

```{python}
#| kind: website
# @title Website version: Fig. 5 with a precomputed slider for the period

```

**Sources.** Data: U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis, national accounts, via FRED: [gross private domestic investment (`GPDI`)](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/GPDI), [net federal government saving (`FGDEF`)](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/FGDEF) and [GDP (`GDP`)](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/GDP).
Prepared file: [`data/ch18/fig18-5.csv`](https://github.com/quarcs-lab/macro102-site/blob/main/data/ch18/fig18-5.csv)
(see the [data notes](https://github.com/quarcs-lab/macro102-site/blob/main/data/ch18/README.md)).
Chart: inspired by Fig. 18.5 in Jones (2024), [*Macroeconomics*, 6th ed.](https://wwnorton.com/books/9781324063612)

<!-- cell -->

**What to notice.**

- Government saving fell: from −2.2 percent of GDP on average in 1960–1979 to −4.1 percent in 1980–2025. Yet
  investment did not fall. It averaged 17.3 percent before 1980 and 17.7 percent after.
- From year to year the two lines move together: from the early 1990s to 2000 government saving rose from −5.1
  (1992) to +1.6 percent of GDP, and investment from 15.3 (1991) to 19.9 percent. In 2009 both fell.
- Click "Private + foreign saving" in the legend. By equation (9) it is the gap between the two lines.
  It rose when deficits grew, to 31.4 percent of GDP in 2020: households, firms and foreigners filled most of
  the gap left by the government, so the crowding out was small.

<!-- cell -->

#### Key numbers: how strongly do the two lines move together?

The textbook speaks of "some correlation in the year-to-year movements". A **correlation** of 1 means two
series move exactly together, 0 means no relation.

> **Python note.** `.diff()` takes the change from the previous year, and `a.corr(b)` is the correlation of two
> Series.

```{python}
I, S = saving_by_year.Investment, saving_by_year["Government saving"]
print(f"Correlation of the levels:            {I.corr(S):.2f}")
print(f"Correlation of the changes each year: {I.diff().corr(S.diff()):.2f}")
for start, end in SPLITS.values():
    print(f"{start}-{end}: investment {period_mean(I, start, end):.2f}%, government saving "
          f"{period_mean(S, start, end):.2f}%, private + foreign saving "
          f"{period_mean(saving_by_year['Private + foreign saving'], start, end):.2f}%")
```

The changes are clearly correlated (0.55), the levels much less (0.29). In the short run, a larger deficit comes
with lower investment. Over decades, private and foreign saving rose by 2.4 points of GDP and covered the larger
deficits. The textbook's estimate is that private saving offsets "no more than 50 cents" of each dollar of
deficit; Chapter 19 looks at the foreign part.

<!-- cell -->

#### Beyond the United States: investment and budget balances in 36 countries

Do the two lines move together in other countries, too? `finance`, from Fig. 1, has private investment and the
general government budget balance (revenue minus spending, called *net lending* in the national accounts) for 36
countries. Private investment is all fixed investment except the government's, plus inventories; for the United
States it is within 0.4 points of GDP of the BEA series above. The budget balance is a little different from
government saving: it also subtracts the government's own investment. The title reports the correlation of the yearly
changes, as in the key numbers above.

```{python}
BALANCE_COUNTRIES = sorted(finance.dropna(subset=["balance", "private_investment"]).country.unique())


def crowding_out_chart(country="United States"):
    """Fig. 18.5 for any country: private investment and the general government budget balance (% of GDP)."""
    rows = finance[finance.country == country].dropna(subset=["balance", "private_investment"])
    rows = rows.rename(columns={"private_investment": "Private investment", "balance": "Budget balance"})
    corr = rows["Private investment"].diff().corr(rows["Budget balance"].diff())
    low, high = -20, 35
    if rows["Budget balance"].min() < -18 or rows["Private investment"].max() > 33:
        low, high = -35, 55                     # a second, fixed scale for the extreme years
    fig = px.line(rows, x="year", y=["Private investment", "Budget balance"], color_discrete_sequence=[BLUE, GREEN],
                  range_x=[1968, 2027], range_y=[low, high],
                  labels={"year": "Year", "value": "Percentage of GDP", "variable": "Series"},
                  title=f"{country}, {rows.year.min()}–{rows.year.max()}: correlation of the yearly changes {corr:.2f}")
    fig.update_traces(line_width=3)
    fig.add_hline(y=0, line=dict(color="black", width=1, dash="dash"))
    fig.update_layout(legend=dict(orientation="h", x=0.99, y=1.02, xanchor="right", yanchor="bottom"),
                      legend_title_text="")
    return fig
```

```{python}
#| kind: widget
interact(crowding_out_chart, country=Dropdown(options=BALANCE_COUNTRIES, value="United States", description="country",
                                              style=WIDE));
```

```{python}
#| kind: website

dropdown_figure(crowding_out_chart, BALANCE_COUNTRIES, start="United States")
```

Prepared file: [`data/ch18/gov_finance.csv`](https://github.com/quarcs-lab/macro102-site/blob/main/data/ch18/gov_finance.csv)
(see the [data notes](https://github.com/quarcs-lab/macro102-site/blob/main/data/ch18/README.md)).
Chart: inspired by Fig. 18.5 in Jones (2024), [*Macroeconomics*, 6th ed.](https://wwnorton.com/books/9781324063612)

<!-- cell -->

Pick a country in the menu above the chart.

**What to notice.**

- With the general government balance, the U.S. correlation of the yearly changes is 0.62, close to the 0.55 of
  the federal measure above.
- The correlation is positive in all 36 countries (median 0.41), from 0.01 in Colombia to 0.75 in Japan. In a
  recession investment falls, and so do tax revenues, while spending rises: both lines drop together. A positive
  correlation therefore does not prove that deficits crowd out investment; the business cycle moves both.
- Choose Ireland: the budget balance fell to −32.2 percent of GDP in 2010, when the government rescued its banks,
  and investment jumped to 51.5 percent of GDP in 2019 for the accounting reason explained in Chapter 17.

## The fiscal problem of the twenty-first century

The last section looks ahead. Official projections show federal spending rising faster than revenue, driven mostly by health care, and health spending is rising in every rich country.

<!-- cell -->

### Fig. 6: U.S. federal spending and revenues, 1950–2075

**Goal.** See the **fiscal problem of the twenty-first century**: entitlement spending keeps rising, while
revenue stays near 18 percent of GDP.

The textbook's figure combines actual data up to 2000 with projections that the Congressional Budget Office (CBO)
made in 2002, up to 2075. Our file has OMB's actual numbers up to FY2025 and CBO's newest long-term projections,
from February 2026, which end in 2056. The column `projection` is 1 for the projected years. Figs. 6 and 7 stay
U.S.-only: they show the CBO's projections, which cover only the U.S. federal budget.

```{python}
projections.tail(3)
```

`ss_medicare_medicaid` is the spending on the three big **entitlement** programs: Social Security, Medicare and
Medicaid (with CHIP and the health insurance tax credits, as CBO counts them). Like the textbook, we draw the
spending excluding interest. We add the textbook's CBO 2002 projections, read from its figure every ten years,
as markers.

```{python}
SERIES = {"revenue": "Revenues", "spending_ex_interest": "Spending excluding interest",
          "ss_medicare_medicaid": "Social Security, Medicare, Medicaid"}
cbo_2002 = pd.DataFrame({"year": [2010, 2020, 2030, 2040, 2050, 2060, 2070, 2075],
                         "Revenues": [19.2, 19.0, 19.0, 19.0, 19.0, 19.0, 19.0, 19.0],
                         "Spending excluding interest": [16.5, 18.5, 21.0, 22.7, 23.7, 25.2, 27.2, 28.2],
                         "Social Security, Medicare, Medicaid": [8.8, 11.3, 13.9, 15.5, 16.5, 18.0, 20.0, 21.1]})
lines = actual_and_projection(projections, SERIES)
lines.head(3)
```

```{python}
COLORS_6 = {"Revenues": GREEN, "Spending excluding interest": DARK_TEAL, "Social Security, Medicare, Medicaid": BLUE}
```

**What to notice.**

- Entitlement spending grew from 0.3 percent of GDP in 1950 to 7.1 percent in 2000 and 11.2 percent in 2025.
  It is now more than half of all non-interest spending, and CBO projects 14.1 percent by 2056.
- Revenue has stayed between 14 and 20 percent of GDP for 75 years, and CBO projects 17.5 to 18.8
  percent. Spending excluding interest stays above it, at about 20 to 21 percent: a **primary deficit** of about
  2 percent of GDP in every projected year.
- The new projection is much flatter than CBO's 2002 projection (the markers): non-interest spending of 21.0
  percent in 2056, against about 24.5 percent projected for the same year in 2002. Click "CBO 2002 (textbook)" to
  hide the markers. But actual spending since 2002 was far above the old projection, in 2009–12 and in 2020–21.

<!-- cell -->

#### What the projection means for the debt

The projected primary deficits are not zero, so the debt keeps growing. How fast the **ratio** grows depends on
the interest rate $i$ and on the growth rate of nominal GDP $g$, through `debt_ratio_path`. The sliders also let
you cut the primary deficit in every year from FY2026, by raising taxes or cutting spending: the two
"possible solutions" of the textbook.

> **Python note.** `max(path)` and `min(path)` are the largest and smallest values of a list, and
> `max(250, ...)` is the larger of two numbers: the vertical axis stays at 0 to 250 unless the debt ratio would
> leave it. `[50, 100, 150, 200, 250] if top == 250 else None` is a one-line `if`: it gives the list of ticks when
> the axis has its usual size, and `None` (let Plotly choose) when it has grown.

```{python}
cbo = projections[projections.projection == 1]
cbo_deficits = (cbo.spending_ex_interest - cbo.revenue).tolist()     # projected primary deficits, FY2026-2056
b_2025 = debt_by_year[2025]
debt_history = debt_deficit[debt_deficit.year >= 1940]


def debt_projection(i=4.0, g=4.0, cut=0.0):
    """The debt ratio after FY2025 under CBO's primary deficits minus a cut (all in percent of GDP)."""
    deficits = []
    for d in cbo_deficits:
        deficits.append(d - cut)
    path = debt_ratio_path(b_2025, i / 100, g / 100, deficits)
    top = max(250, 1.05 * max(path))                 # fixed axis, widened only when the debt ratio would leave it
    bottom = min(0, 1.1 * min(path))                 # below zero, the government owns more than it owes
    fig = px.line(debt_history, x="year", y="debt_public_gdp_pct", range_y=[bottom, top],
                  labels={"year": "Fiscal year", "debt_public_gdp_pct": "Debt held by the public (% of GDP)"},
                  title=f"Debt in FY2056: {path[-1]:.1f}% of GDP (FY2025: {b_2025:.1f}%), "
                        f"average primary deficit {np.mean(deficits):.2f}%")
    fig.update_traces(line=dict(color=BLUE, width=3))
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=cbo.year, y=path, name="Projection", line=dict(color=BLUE, width=3, dash="dash"),
                             showlegend=False))
    fig.add_hline(y=b_2025, line=dict(color=GRAY, width=1, dash="dot"))
    fig.add_vrect(x0=2025, x1=2056, fillcolor=GRAY, opacity=0.12, line_width=0)
    fig.update_xaxes(range=[1938, 2058])
    fig.update_yaxes(tickvals=[50, 100, 150, 200, 250] if top == 250 else None)
    return fig
```

```{python}
#| kind: widget
interact(debt_projection,
         i=FloatSlider(value=4.0, min=0.0, max=8.0, step=0.5, description="interest rate i (%)", style=WIDE),
         g=FloatSlider(value=4.0, min=0.0, max=8.0, step=0.5, description="nominal GDP growth g (%)", style=WIDE),
         cut=FloatSlider(value=0.0, min=0.0, max=4.0, step=0.5, description="deficit cut (% of GDP)", style=WIDE));
```

```{python}

# @title Website version: the debt projection with a precomputed slider for the deficit cut (i = g = 4%)
slider_figure(debt_projection, "cut", [0.0, 0.5, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0, 2.5, 3.0], start=0.0, label="deficit cut (% of GDP)")
```

**Sources.** Data: [Office of Management and Budget, Historical Tables](https://www.whitehouse.gov/omb/budget/historical-tables/), Table 7.1 (debt held by the public); [Congressional Budget Office, *The Long-Term Budget Outlook: 2026 to 2056*](https://www.cbo.gov/data/budget-economic-data) (primary deficits, revenue minus spending excluding interest).
Prepared files: [`data/ch18/fig18-2.csv`](https://github.com/quarcs-lab/macro102-site/blob/main/data/ch18/fig18-2.csv), [`data/ch18/fig18-6.csv`](https://github.com/quarcs-lab/macro102-site/blob/main/data/ch18/fig18-6.csv)
(see the [data notes](https://github.com/quarcs-lab/macro102-site/blob/main/data/ch18/README.md)).
Chart: inspired by the discussion of Fig. 18.6 in Jones (2024), [*Macroeconomics*, 6th ed.](https://wwnorton.com/books/9781324063612)

<!-- cell -->

**What to notice.**

- With $i = g$ the interest and growth effects cancel, and the ratio simply adds up the primary deficits: from
  99.5 percent of GDP in FY2025 to about 164 percent in FY2056.
- Set the interest rate one point above growth ($i = 5$, $g = 4$): the debt now grows faster than GDP even
  without deficits, and the ratio ends at 209 percent. One point below ($i = 3$), the same deficits give 130
  percent. This is the "magic elixir" of growth from Fig. 2, working in either direction.
- With $i = g$, a cut of about 2 percent of GDP in every year, the size of the average primary deficit, keeps
  the ratio near its FY2025 level.

### Fig. 8: Health spending as a share of GDP in five countries

**Goal.** Show that the rise of health spending is not only a U.S. problem.

The data are the total current health expenditure, public and private, as a percentage of GDP, from the OECD
Health Statistics.

```{python}

health.isna().sum()
```

Some values are missing: France reports only every five years before 1990, and Germany has no value for 1991,
the year after reunification. If we plotted the wide table, France's line would have holes. After `melt`, we
drop the missing rows with `.dropna()`, so that each line connects the years that do exist. The OECD's current
data start in 1970, so the textbook's points for 1960 and 1965 cannot be drawn, and the 2025 values are
provisional estimates.

```{python}
fig = px.line(health_long, x="year", y="health_share", color="country", hover_name="country", range_y=[2, 20],
              color_discrete_map={"U.S.": BLUE, "Germany": DARK_TEAL, "France": GREEN, "Japan": ORANGE,
                                  "U.K.": LIGHT_BLUE},

fig.update_traces(line_width=3)
```

**Source.** Data: OECD Health Statistics, System of Health Accounts, current health expenditure as a percentage of GDP (dataflow `DSD_SHA@DF_SHA`), via the [OECD Data Explorer](https://data-explorer.oecd.org/).
Prepared file: [`data/ch18/fig18-8.csv`](https://github.com/quarcs-lab/macro102-site/blob/main/data/ch18/fig18-8.csv)
(see the [data notes](https://github.com/quarcs-lab/macro102-site/blob/main/data/ch18/README.md)).

<!-- cell -->

**What to notice.**

- Health spending rose in all five countries, as a share of GDP. In the U.S. it nearly tripled, from 6.2
  percent in 1970 to 17.6 percent in 2025. The average of the other four rose from 4.8 to about 11–12 percent.
- The U.S. pulled away from the others in the 1980s. Since 2010 its share has stayed near 16–18 percent. Japan
  and the U.K., the lowest spenders until 2010, came close to Germany and France.
- The pandemic shows as a spike in 2020 (U.S. 18.7 percent, U.K. 12.0 percent): health spending rose and GDP
  fell at the same time.

<!-- cell -->

#### Key numbers: why health spending rises

```{python}
first_year, last_year = health.set_index("year").loc[1970], health.set_index("year").loc[2025]
growth = 100 * ((last_year / first_year) ** (1 / 55) - 1)        # average growth of the share, percent a year
pd.DataFrame({"1970": first_year, "2021": health.set_index("year").loc[2021], "2025": last_year,
              "Share growth, % a year": growth}).round(2)
```

The share of GDP spent on health grew by between 1.4 and 1.9 percent a year in every country: health spending
grew faster than income. The textbook's explanation is economic: as people get richer, an extra car or television
adds less and less, but an extra year of life does not lose its value. So a rising share of income goes to
health. That is why the fiscal problem is hard. If health spending is what people want, the government cannot
simply cut it, and someone has to pay for it.

## Concluding remarks

- The U.S. federal government spends about 23 percent of GDP and collects about 17 percent. The deficit, about
  6 percent of GDP in recent years, is financed by selling bonds, and the debt held by the public is back near
  100 percent of GDP, the level of 1946.
- The **flow budget constraint**, equations (1) and (2), links each year's deficit to the change in the debt.
  The **intertemporal budget constraint**, equations (3) and (4), says that the budget must balance in present
  value: borrowing today means surpluses, and higher taxes, later.
- What matters is the debt relative to GDP. Its law of motion, equations (5) and (6), shows that when GDP grows
  faster than the interest rate, the ratio falls even without surpluses: that is how the United States paid
  down its World War II debt. When the interest rate is above growth, only primary surpluses as large as
  equation (7) keep the ratio from rising, and the closed form, equation (8), shows the ratio exploding otherwise.
- The saving-investment identity, equation (9), says that a deficit must be financed by private or foreign
  saving, or it crowds out investment (equation 10).
- U.S. government spending is low compared with other rich countries, and its debt ratio is typical. Large
  deficits have not lowered the U.S. investment rate, because private and foreign saving rose.
- The fiscal problem of the twenty-first century is the rise of health spending, in the U.S. and in every rich
  country: by equation (11), aging and costs that grow faster than income both raise its share of GDP. Chapter 19 turns to the international economy, including the foreign saving that has financed much
  of the U.S. deficit.

### Conceptual problems

<!-- cell -->

**Problem 1 (Basic): Who lends to the German government?** In 2025 Germany reformed its constitutional debt brake, the rule that limits government borrowing. The IMF's [2025 Article IV press release on Germany](https://www.imf.org/en/news/articles/2026/02/11/pr26042-germany-imf-executive-board-concludes-2025-article-iv-consultation) projects a general government balance of −2.4 percent of GDP for 2025 and −3.4 percent for 2026, while the current account surplus shrinks from 4.5 to 4.0 percent of GDP. Foreign saving is minus the current account balance: a country with a surplus lends to the rest of the world.

(a) In our data (`gov_finance.csv`, from the OECD national accounts via the [OECD Data Explorer](https://data-explorer.oecd.org/), the file behind the country menus of Figs. 1 and 5), Germany's private investment was 17.6 percent of GDP in 2024 and its budget balance −2.6 percent. The same IMF release puts the 2024 current account surplus at 5.8 percent of GDP. Use equation (9) to compute German private saving in 2024.

(b) Suppose the 2026 projections come true and private saving stays at the same share of GDP. By how much does private investment change from 2025 to 2026? Which values of $\theta$ and $\phi$ in equation (10) describe this case?

(c) What would private saving have to do for investment not to fall at all?

<details><summary>Hint</summary>

In equation (9), government saving is the budget balance $T - G$ and foreign saving is $IM - EX$, which is minus the current account. For (b), take the change of every term of equation (9) from 2025 to 2026, and watch the signs: a larger deficit is a fall in government saving, and a smaller current account surplus is a rise in foreign saving.

</details>

<!-- cell -->

**Your answer:**

<!-- cell -->

<details><summary>Solution</summary>

**(a)** Solve equation (9) for private saving:

$$Y - T - C = I - (T - G) - (IM - EX) = 17.6 - (-2.6) - (-5.8) = 26.0 \text{ percent of GDP}.$$

German households and firms saved 26.0 percent of GDP. Only 17.6 points financed private investment at home: 2.6 points went to the government's deficit and 5.8 points were lent abroad. (The budget balance in our file is *net lending*, which already subtracts the government's own investment. That is why it pairs with *private* investment in the identity.)

**(b)** Take changes of equation (9). Private saving does not change, government saving falls by 1.0 point ($-3.4 - (-2.4)$) and foreign saving rises by 0.5 point (the surplus falls from 4.5 to 4.0):

$$\Delta I = 0 + (-1.0) + 0.5 = -0.5 \text{ point of GDP}.$$

This is equation (10) with $\Delta = 1$, $\theta = 0$ and $\phi = 0.5$: $\Delta I = -(1 - 0 - 0.5) \times 1 = -0.5$. Half of the extra deficit is financed by lending less abroad, and the other half crowds out private investment.

**(c)** Investment does not fall when $\theta + \phi = 1$, so with $\phi = 0.5$ private saving must rise by $\theta\Delta = 0.5$ point of GDP. That happens if households save part of their higher incomes, or save for the higher taxes they expect later (Ricardian equivalence).

*Interpretation.* Because Germany starts with a large current account surplus, much of its new borrowing can come from saving that now goes abroad, so crowding out can be small. Equation (9) is an identity, though: it says how the deficit must be financed, not why. The projected fall in the surplus could also come from higher investment rather than from the deficit.

</details>

<!-- cell -->

**Problem 2 (Intermediate): Greece in 2011: could any surplus have stopped the debt?** At the end of 2010, Greece's gross government debt was 147.85 percent of GDP (`gross_debt.csv`, from the IMF's [*Public Finances in Modern History*](https://www.imf.org/external/datamapper/datasets/FPP) database, as in Fig. 2). In 2011 investors lost confidence: the yield on 10-year Greek government bonds averaged 15.75 percent ([OECD, via FRED, series `IRLTLT01GRM156N`](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/IRLTLT01GRM156N)), and nominal GDP fell by 9.0 percent ([World Bank, GDP in current local currency, `NY.GDP.MKTP.CN`](https://data.worldbank.org/indicator/NY.GDP.MKTP.CN?locations=GR)).

(a) Suppose the whole debt paid the 2011 market yield. Use equation (7) to compute the primary surplus that would have held the debt ratio at 147.85 percent of GDP in 2011. Compare it with Greek government revenue, which was 44.6 percent of GDP in 2011 (`gov_finance.csv`).

(b) Now suppose the interest rate were zero. What primary surplus would still have been needed? What does this say about the role of growth?

(c) In our data, the ratio rose to 175.1 percent of GDP in 2011, and fell to 164.3 percent in 2012, the year in which Greece restructured its privately held bonds ([Zettelmeyer, Trebesch and Gulati 2013](https://doi.org/10.1111/1468-0327.12014)). Use the "confidence and default" argument of the Model overview to explain why a high debt can become impossible to stabilize, and why lowering the interest rate on the debt had to be part of the solution.

<details><summary>Hint</summary>

Write both rates as decimals: $i = 0.1575$ and $g = -0.090$. A falling GDP makes $i - g$ *larger* than $i$. For (c), follow a rise in $i$ through equation (7), and ask what a larger required surplus does to the lenders' belief that they will be repaid.

</details>

<!-- cell -->

**Your answer:**

<!-- cell -->

<details><summary>Solution</summary>

**(a)** Equation (7) with $i = 0.1575$, $g = -0.090$ and $b = 147.85$:

$$-d = \frac{i-g}{1+g}\,b = \frac{0.1575 - (-0.090)}{1 - 0.090} \times 147.85 = \frac{0.2475}{0.910} \times 147.85 = 0.272 \times 147.85 = 40.2 \text{ percent of GDP}.$$

With revenue of 44.6 percent of GDP, a primary surplus of 40.2 percent would have left only 4.4 percent of GDP for all spending other than interest: no schools, no pensions, no police. No government can do that.

**(b)** With $i = 0$:

$$-d = \frac{0 - (-0.090)}{1 - 0.090} \times 147.85 = \frac{0.090}{0.910} \times 147.85 = 14.6 \text{ percent of GDP}.$$

Even free borrowing would have required a surplus of 14.6 percent of GDP, because a shrinking GDP raises the ratio by itself: the denominator falls. In equation (7), a fall in $g$ weighs as much as a rise in $i$. Growth is the "magic elixir" of Fig. 2 in reverse.

**(c)** When lenders start to doubt repayment, they ask for a higher $i$. By equation (7), a higher $i$ raises the surplus needed to stop the ratio from rising. Raising that surplus means tax increases and spending cuts, which lower GDP in the short run, so $g$ falls as well. The required surplus grows again, repayment looks even less likely, and lenders ask for a still higher rate. The fear fulfills itself: at a yield of 15.75 percent and a shrinking GDP, no feasible primary surplus could stabilize the ratio. The way out is to lower $i$ or the debt itself, by a restructuring (a partial default, as in 2012) or by borrowing from official lenders instead of the market. The ratio fell from 175.1 to 164.3 percent in 2012 even though GDP kept falling, because the restructuring cut the face value of the debt.

One detail: only *new* bonds pay the market yield, while old bonds keep the rate at which they were sold. The average rate on the whole debt was therefore much lower than 15.75 percent, and (a) is an upper bound. That is also why the ratio rose by 27.2 points in 2011, primary deficit included, and not by the 40.2 points that interest minus growth alone would have added at the market yield.

</details>

**Problem 3 (Challenge): Norway's oil fund and the generations to come.** Norway's government owns far more than it owes: in our data (`net_debt.csv`, the OECD's government balance sheets via the [OECD Data Explorer](https://data-explorer.oecd.org/), as in Fig. 4), its net debt was −413.8 percent of GDP in 2024, most of it the oil fund. Norway's [fiscal rule](https://norskpetroleum.no/en/economy/management-of-revenues/) says that, over time, the budget may spend only the fund's expected real return, now estimated at 3 percent a year, and never the fund itself. Work in real terms: by the inflation argument of the Model overview, replace $i$ by the real return $r = 3\%$ and $g$ by real GDP growth, which we *assume* is 1.5 percent a year (an illustrative value, not a forecast). Treat all net assets as one fund, and leave out new oil revenue.

(a) Rewrite equation (4) for a government that starts with assets, $B_1 < 0$. What does it allow the government to do?

(b) Under the 3 percent rule, how large is the primary deficit (spending above non-oil taxes) in the first year, 2025? Give it in percent of that year's GDP, as $d_t$ in equation (5); the fund's 413.8 percent is measured against the GDP of 2024. What happens to the real value of the fund, and to its ratio to GDP after 30 years?

(c) Use equation (7) to find the primary deficit that would keep the fund at 413.8 percent of GDP forever.

(d) The deficit allowed by the 3 percent rule shrinks as a share of GDP. After how many years does it fall below the deficit of (c)? Which rule treats future generations better? (This last question has no single right answer: argue for one.)

<details><summary>Hint</summary>

For (a), look at the sign of the right side of equation (4) when $B_1 < 0$. For (b), spending exactly the real return leaves the fund's real value unchanged, while real GDP grows 1.5 percent a year, already in the first year. For (c), put $b = -413.8$ into equation (7) and read the sign of $d$. For (d), compare the two deficits in the first year, then ask how long it takes GDP to grow by that factor; the rule of 70 gives a quick answer.

</details>

<!-- cell -->

**Your answer:**

<!-- cell -->

<details><summary>Solution</summary>

**(a)** With $B_1 < 0$, equation (4) reads

$$(T_1 - G_1) + \frac{T_2 - G_2}{1+i} = (1+i)B_1 < 0.$$

The present value of the budget balances is *negative*: the government may run primary deficits, as long as their present value equals its assets plus the interest on them, $(1+i)\lvert B_1\rvert$. With many periods it can do so forever: a deficit equal to the return on the fund leaves the fund intact.

**(b)** The first-year deficit is the real return on the fund, $0.03 \times 413.8 = 12.4$ percent of 2024 GDP. Equation (5) divides it by the GDP of 2025, which is 1.5 percent larger:

$$d_{2025} = \frac{0.03 \times 413.8}{1.015} = \frac{12.4}{1.015} = 12.2 \text{ percent of GDP}.$$

The fund's real value does not change, but real GDP grows, so the ratio shrinks by the growth rule for a ratio, $g_b = 0 - 1.5\%$:

$$\frac{413.8}{1.015^{30}} = 264.7 \text{ percent of GDP after 30 years},$$

and the deficit the rule allows in that thirtieth year is $0.03 \times 264.7 = 7.9$ percent of that year's GDP.

**(c)** Equation (7) in real terms, with $b = -413.8$:

$$-d = \frac{r - g}{1+g}\,b = \frac{0.03 - 0.015}{1.015} \times (-413.8) = -6.1, \qquad\text{so } d = 6.1 \text{ percent of GDP}.$$

A permanent primary deficit of 6.1 percent of GDP keeps the assets at 413.8 percent of GDP. Check with the steady state: $b^* = \frac{1+g}{g-r}\,d = \frac{1.015}{-0.015} \times 6.115 = -413.8$.

**(d)** The 3 percent rule's first deficit, 12.2 percent of GDP from (b), is exactly twice the 6.1 percent of (c), since $r/(r-g) = 0.03/0.015 = 2$. Its deficit shrinks with the ratio, at the rate of real growth, so it falls to the level of (c) once GDP has doubled from its level in the first year. By the rule of 70 that takes about $70/1.5 \approx 47$ years ($\ln 2 / \ln 1.015 = 46.6$ exactly): the rule's deficit is larger than that of (c) in each of the first 47 years and smaller from the 48th year on.

- The 3 percent rule gives every generation the **same real amount** (in kroner of today's value). The generations living in the next half century get more than under the rule of (c), and those after them less, as a share of their (larger) incomes.
- The constant-ratio rule gives every generation the **same share of GDP**. It spends less today and lets the fund grow with the economy.

Future generations will be richer, which is an argument for spending more now (the 3 percent rule). Expected returns are uncertain, which is an argument for spending less (if the real return turns out lower than 3 percent, the 3 percent rule eats into the fund). The arithmetic of equations (4) and (7) shows the trade-off; choosing between the two rules is a value judgment. In reality the fund has kept growing: Norway's net debt was −154.9 percent of GDP in 2011 and −413.8 percent in 2024 in our data. According to the page linked above, the state's net oil revenue is paid into the fund every year (this problem leaves it out), and the fund's investments have earned large returns.

</details>

**Problem 4 (Basic): How much of each tax dollar goes to interest?** The file `federal_budget.csv`, which we built from the [Office of Management and Budget's Historical Tables](https://www.whitehouse.gov/omb/budget/historical-tables/), has the lines of Table 18.1 for every fiscal year from 1940 to 2025, in percent of GDP.

(a) In FY2025, how many cents of each dollar of federal revenue went to net interest?

(b) Is that a record since FY1940? Which earlier years came close, and why was interest so high then? (Fig. 2 helps.)

(c) In which fiscal years was net interest larger than defense spending?

<details><summary>Hint</summary>

Keep the rows with `release == "actual (FY2027 Budget)"`, so that each year appears once, and make `year` the index. Both `net_interest` and `total_revenue` are in percent of GDP, so `100 * net_interest / total_revenue` is the number of cents per dollar of revenue. `.sort_values(ascending=False).head()` lists the largest values.

</details>

```{python}
# Your answer here
```

<details><summary>Solution</summary>

We keep the actual numbers, divide net interest by revenue, rank the years, and compare interest with defense.

```python
fed = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "federal_budget.csv")
fed = fed[fed.release == "actual (FY2027 Budget)"].set_index("year")
cents = 100 * fed.net_interest / fed.total_revenue      # cents of interest per dollar of revenue
print(f"FY2025: {cents[2025]:.1f} cents of each dollar of revenue went to net interest")
print("The five highest years:")
print(cents.sort_values(ascending=False).head().round(1))
print(f"Lowest since 1980: {cents.loc[1980:].min():.1f} cents in FY{cents.loc[1980:].idxmin()}")

```

- **(a)** In FY2025, 18.5 cents of each dollar of federal revenue paid the interest on the debt.
- **(b)** It is the highest share since FY1940, but only just: FY1991 had 18.4 cents, FY1992 18.3 cents and FY1990 17.9 cents, and FY2024 also had 17.9 cents. Around 1990 the debt had grown fast (from 25.5 percent of GDP in FY1980 to 47.9 percent in FY1993, Fig. 2) while interest rates were high. The lowest share since 1980 was 6.9 cents in FY2015: the debt was large (72.2 percent of GDP), but interest rates were very low. The interest bill depends on the debt *and* on the interest rate.
- **(c)** Only in FY2024 and FY2025. In our data, which start in FY1940, the federal government had never before paid more in interest than for its military.

**Problem 5 (Intermediate): Big government, big debt?** Is it true that countries with large governments also have large debts? Use the 2024 general government spending of `gov_spending.csv` (from the OECD's *Government at a Glance*, via the [OECD Data Explorer](https://data-explorer.oecd.org/)), the 2024 gross debt of `gross_debt.csv` (from the IMF's [*Public Finances in Modern History*](https://www.imf.org/external/datamapper/datasets/FPP) database) and the budget balances of `gov_finance.csv` (OECD national accounts).

(a) Put each country's 2024 spending and gross debt side by side. How many countries have both, and what is the correlation between the two?

(b) List the countries that spend more than 47 percent of GDP but owe less than 60 percent of GDP, and those that spend less than 40 percent of GDP but owe more than 100 percent.

(c) Now average each country's budget balance over 2000–2024 and correlate it with the 2024 gross debt. Explain the difference between (a) and (c) with the flow budget constraint, equation (2).

<details><summary>Hint</summary>

The files spell some countries differently ("U.S." in one, "United States" in the other), so match them on the three-letter code `iso3`. For (c), `groupby("iso3").balance.mean()` gives one average per country, and `pd.concat([first, second], axis=1).dropna()` lines up two Series by their country code.

</details>

```{python}
# Your answer here
```

<details><summary>Solution</summary>

We merge the two 2024 tables on `iso3`, then filter the corners of the scatter, then repeat with the average balance.

```python
spend = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "gov_spending.csv")
debt_all = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "gross_debt.csv")
both = spend[spend.year == 2024].merge(debt_all[debt_all.year == 2024][["iso3", "gross_debt"]], on="iso3")
print(f"(a) {len(both)} countries, correlation {both.gov_spending.corr(both.gross_debt):.2f}")
big_low = both[(both.gov_spending > 47) & (both.gross_debt < 60)]
small_high = both[(both.gov_spending < 40) & (both.gross_debt > 100)]
print(big_low[["country", "gov_spending", "gross_debt"]].round(2).to_string(index=False))
print(small_high[["country", "gov_spending", "gross_debt"]].round(2).to_string(index=False))

fin_all = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "gov_finance.csv")
recent = fin_all[(fin_all.year >= 2000) & (fin_all.year <= 2024)]
average_balance = recent.groupby("iso3").balance.mean()
debt_2024 = debt_all[debt_all.year == 2024].set_index("iso3").gross_debt
pair = pd.concat([average_balance, debt_2024], axis=1).dropna()
print(f"(c) {len(pair)} countries, correlation {pair.balance.corr(pair.gross_debt):.2f}")
```

- **(a)** 36 countries have both numbers, and the correlation is only 0.19: the size of government says little about its debt.
- **(b)** Six countries spend more than 47 percent of GDP but owe less than 60 percent: Denmark (47.33 and 31.45 percent), Iceland, Norway, Poland, Slovakia and Sweden (50.47 and 32.99). Two spend less than 40 percent but owe more than 100 percent: Japan (38.73 and 236.66) and the United States (39.57 and 122.32).
- **(c)** Across 39 countries, the correlation between the average balance of 2000–2024 and the 2024 debt is −0.52: countries with larger deficits (more negative balances) owe more. By equation (2), the debt grows by the primary deficit $G_t - T_t$ plus interest. What builds up debt is the *gap* between spending and taxes, not the level of spending. Sweden and Denmark spend a lot, but they also tax a lot; Japan and the United States spend less but have taxed even less, year after year.

</details>

**Problem 6 (Intermediate): Do countries with bigger deficits invest less?** If deficits crowd out investment, equation (10), countries with larger deficits over many years should have lower investment rates. Use the general government balance and private investment of `gov_finance.csv` (OECD national accounts, via the [OECD Data Explorer](https://data-explorer.oecd.org/)).

(a) For each country, average the budget balance and private investment over 2000–2019, the twenty years before the pandemic. What is the correlation across countries? Does its sign fit the crowding-out story?

(b) Name one country that fits the story well and two that clearly do not.

(c) Why is this comparison across countries a weak test of equation (10)? Name two reasons.

<details><summary>Hint</summary>

First drop the rows where either column is missing with `.dropna(subset=["balance", "private_investment"])`, then use `groupby("country")[["balance", "private_investment"]].mean()`. Crowding out means that a *lower* balance (a bigger deficit) comes with *lower* investment, so it predicts a positive correlation.

</details>

```{python}
# Your answer here
```

**Your answer:**

<!-- cell -->

<details><summary>Solution</summary>

We average each country over 2000–2019, then correlate the averages and look at the extremes. `np.polyfit(x, y, 1)` fits a straight line and returns its slope first.

```python
fin_all = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "gov_finance.csv")
pre_covid = fin_all[(fin_all.year >= 2000) & (fin_all.year <= 2019)]
pre_covid = pre_covid.dropna(subset=["balance", "private_investment"])
means = pre_covid.groupby("country")[["balance", "private_investment"]].mean()
slope = np.polyfit(means.balance, means.private_investment, 1)[0]
print(f"{len(means)} countries: correlation {means.balance.corr(means.private_investment):.2f}, slope {slope:.2f}")
print("Largest deficits:")
print(means.sort_values("balance").head().round(1))
print("Highest investment rates:")
print(means.sort_values("private_investment", ascending=False).head(3).round(1))
```

- **(a)** Across 36 countries the correlation is 0.14, and the fitted slope is 0.26: one point of GDP more in average deficit comes with only 0.26 point less investment. The sign fits crowding out, but the relation is weak; most of the differences in investment have nothing to do with the budget.
- **(b)** Greece fits the story: the largest average deficit (−6.5 percent of GDP) and the lowest investment rate (14.3 percent). South Korea fits it too, with an average surplus of 1.5 percent of GDP and high investment, 26.8 percent. The United States does not: it has the second-largest deficit, −6.1 percent of GDP, but an average investment rate of 17.7 percent. Nor does China, which invests by far the most, 36.6 percent of GDP, with an average deficit of 2.0 percent of GDP.
- **(c)** First, equation (10) allows private and foreign saving to fill the gap: in open economies, foreigners can finance a deficit ($\phi > 0$), as Fig. 5 suggests they did for the United States. Second, many other things differ across countries: households' saving habits (very high in China), demography, the stage of development, and the business cycle, which moves deficits and investment at the same time. A correlation across countries cannot separate these forces from the effect of the deficit.

</details>

**Problem 7 (Challenge): Interest rates, growth and the U.S. debt, FY1950–2025.** Equation (5) says that the debt ratio grows by the factor $(1+i)/(1+g)$, plus the primary deficit. Here you measure $i$ and $g$ for the United States, year by year. Use `federal_budget.csv` (fiscal-year GDP in billions of dollars, net interest and the budget balance in percent of GDP) and the debt held by the public at the end of each fiscal year in `fig18-2.csv` (both from the [OMB Historical Tables](https://www.whitehouse.gov/omb/budget/historical-tables/)).

(a) Compute the **effective interest rate** of each year, net interest divided by the debt at the start of the year, and the growth rate of nominal GDP. In how many years from FY1950 to FY2025 was $i$ below $g$, and what was the average gap $i - g$?

(b) Average $i$ and $g$ by decade. In which decades was $i$ above $g$? How does that fit the path of the debt ratio in Fig. 2?

(c) What were $i$, $g$ and $i - g$ in FY2022? Explain the number with the inflation argument of the Model overview.

(d) Use equation (5), with your $i$, $g$ and the primary deficit, to predict each year's debt ratio from the year before, and compare with the actual ratio for FY2019–2025. Which years does equation (5) miss by more than 2 points?

<details><summary>Hint</summary>

The debt at the start of year $t$ is the debt at the end of year $t-1$: in dollars, `debt_ratio / 100 * GDP`, then `.shift(1)`. Net interest in dollars is `net_interest / 100 * GDP`. The primary deficit, in percent of GDP, is the total deficit minus interest: `-balance - net_interest`. Compute every column before you keep the years 1950–2025, so that FY1950 has a previous year.

</details>

```{python}
# Your answer here
```

**Your answer:**

<!-- cell -->

<details><summary>Solution</summary>

We line up the two files by year, compute the debt in dollars, the effective rate, growth and the primary deficit, and then apply equation (5).

```python
fed = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "federal_budget.csv")
fed = fed[fed.release == "actual (FY2027 Budget)"].set_index("year")
debt_end = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "fig18-2.csv").set_index("year").debt_public_gdp_pct
rates = pd.DataFrame({"Y": fed.gdp_billions, "b": debt_end})
rates["B"] = rates.b / 100 * rates.Y                          # debt at the end of the year, billions of dollars
rates["i"] = fed.net_interest * rates.Y / rates.B.shift(1)    # interest paid / debt at the start, percent
rates["g"] = 100 * (rates.Y / rates.Y.shift(1) - 1)
rates["d"] = -fed.balance - fed.net_interest                  # primary deficit, percent of GDP
rates["predicted"] = (1 + rates.i / 100) / (1 + rates.g / 100) * rates.b.shift(1) + rates.d   # equation (5)
rates = rates.loc[1950:2025]
gap = rates.i - rates.g
print(f"(a) i < g in {(gap < 0).sum()} of {len(rates)} years; average i - g {gap.mean():.2f} points")
for start in range(1950, 2030, 10):
    part = rates.loc[start:start + 9]
    print(f"(b) {start}s: i {part.i.mean():.2f}%, g {part.g.mean():.2f}%")
print(f"(c) FY2022: i {rates.i[2022]:.2f}%, g {rates.g[2022]:.2f}%, i - g {gap[2022]:.2f}; rank {int(gap.rank()[2022])} of {len(gap)}")
print(rates.loc[2019:2025, ["i", "g", "d", "b", "predicted"]].round(2))
```

- **(a)** The effective rate was below nominal growth in 48 of the 76 years, and on average 1.64 points below it. That is the "magic elixir" of the Model overview: most of the time, the United States outgrew its debt.
- **(b)** By decade, $i$ was far below $g$ in the 1950s (2.31 against 6.29 percent), the 1960s and the 1970s, when the debt ratio fell from its war peak to 23.2 percent of GDP (FY1974). It was **above** $g$ in the 1980s (9.13 against 8.05 percent), the 1990s (6.93 against 5.49) and, narrowly, the 2000s (4.81 against 4.35). In those decades the term $(i-g)\,b$ pushed the ratio up, on top of the deficits of the 1980s. Since 2010 $i$ is again below $g$: 2.12 against 3.94 percent in the 2010s, and 2.56 against 6.13 percent in 2020–2025.
- **(c)** In FY2022, $i = 2.14$ percent and $g = 10.94$ percent, so $i - g = -8.81$ points, the second-lowest value since 1950, after FY1951. Inflation surged in 2021–22 ([Chapter 8](https://quarcs-lab.github.io/macro102-site/notebooks/ch08-inflation.html)), so nominal GDP grew fast, while most of the debt had been sold earlier at low fixed rates. Unexpected inflation lowered the real value of the debt, as the Model overview predicts: the ratio fell from 96.7 to 94.9 percent although the primary deficit was 3.51 percent of GDP.
- **(d)** Equation (5) predicts the ratio within about 1 point in FY2019 and FY2023–2025, but it misses by 5.28 points in FY2020 (predicted 93.22, actual 98.5), by −6.54 points in FY2021 (103.24 against 96.7) and by 2.36 points in FY2022. In those years the Treasury did not borrow exactly its deficit. It borrowed more than it needed in FY2020 and held the cash at the Federal Reserve, where its balance rose from about 0.3 trillion dollars in September 2019 to 1.7 trillion in September 2020; it spent the cash down to 0.2 trillion by September 2021, and raised it to 0.7 trillion by September 2022 ([Federal Reserve Board, H.4.1, U.S. Treasury General Account, week averages, via FRED, `WTREGEN`](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/WTREGEN)). The flow budget constraint holds once we count changes in the government's cash as a use of funds. Our $i$ is also approximate: net interest is interest paid minus some interest received.

</details>

**Problem 8 (Basic): Can France meet the EU's debt rule?** France's gross government debt was 113.15 percent of GDP in 2024 (`gross_debt.csv`). Under the EU's reformed fiscal rules of 2024, the debt ratio of a country above 90 percent of GDP must fall by at least 1 point of GDP a year on average, in plans that run four to seven years ([European Parliament Research Service, 2024](https://www.europarl.europa.eu/RegData/etudes/ATAG/2024/760429/EPRS_ATA%282024%29760429_EN.pdf)). The calculator below starts from France's 2024 ratio and runs four years of equation (5), with nominal GDP growth fixed at $g = 3\%$ (an illustrative value).

(a) With an interest rate of $i = 3\%$, which constant primary balance meets the rule exactly?

(b) If lenders demand $i = 4\%$ instead, how large must the yearly primary surplus be?

<details><summary>Hint</summary>

The slider sets the primary deficit $d$; a negative value is a surplus. Move it until the title shows an average change of −1.00 point a year, or as close as the slider allows. Before you move it, use equation (6) to predict the answer to (a).

</details>

```{python}
#| kind: widget
b_france = gross[(gross.country == "France") & (gross.year == 2024)].gross_debt.iloc[0]


def eu_debt_rule(i=3.0, g=3.0, d=0.0):
    """Equation (5) for four years from France's 2024 debt ratio, with a constant primary deficit d."""
    path = [b_france] + debt_ratio_path(b_france, i / 100, g / 100, [d] * 4)
    rule = []
    for t in range(5):
        rule.append(b_france - t)                # the EU minimum: 1 point of GDP less each year
    average = round((path[-1] - b_france) / 4, 2) + 0.0
    fig = go.Figure()
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=list(range(2024, 2029)), y=rule, mode="lines", name="EU rule: −1 point a year",
                             line=dict(color=GRAY, width=2, dash="dash")))
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=list(range(2024, 2029)), y=path, mode="lines+markers", name="Debt ratio",
                             line=dict(color=BLUE, width=3)))
    fig.update_layout(title=f"Average change {average:+.2f} points a year: {path[-1]:.2f}% of GDP in 2028",
                      xaxis=dict(title="Year", tickvals=[2024, 2025, 2026, 2027, 2028]),
                      yaxis=dict(title="Gross debt (% of GDP)", range=[90, 130]),
                      legend=dict(x=0.01, y=0.99, xanchor="left", yanchor="top"))
    return fig


interact(eu_debt_rule,
         i=FloatSlider(value=3.0, min=2.0, max=5.0, step=0.5, description="interest rate i (%)", style=WIDE),
         g=fixed(3.0),
         d=FloatSlider(value=0.0, min=-4.0, max=1.0, step=0.1, description="primary deficit d (% of GDP)",
                       style=WIDE));
```

**Source.** A calculator built on the debt-ratio tools of the Model overview, equations (5) and (6), adapted from the discussion of the debt-GDP ratio in Chapter 18 of Jones (2024), [*Macroeconomics*, 6th ed.](https://wwnorton.com/books/9781324063612)

```{python}
# Your answer here
```

<details><summary>Solution</summary>

**(a)** With $i = g$, the term $\frac{i-g}{1+g}\,b$ of equation (6) is zero, so the ratio changes by exactly the primary deficit: $b_t - b_{t-1} = d_t$. A primary surplus of 1.0 percent of GDP ($d = -1.0$) meets the rule exactly, and the slider confirms it: an average change of −1.00 point a year, to 109.15 percent of GDP in 2028.

**(b)** With $i = 4\%$, interest adds $\frac{0.04 - 0.03}{1.03} \times 113.15 = 1.10$ points to the ratio in the first year, so the surplus must cover that as well: about $1 + 1.10 = 2.1$ percent of GDP. On the slider, $d = -2.1$ gives an average change of −1.02 point a year, and $d = -2.0$ only −0.91. The exact constant surplus is 2.08 percent of GDP (a little less than 2.10, because the debt, and with it the interest effect, falls along the way):

```python
for d in [-2.0, -2.08, -2.1]:
    path = debt_ratio_path(b_france, 0.04, 0.03, [d] * 4)
    print(f"d = {d}: debt in 2028 {path[-1]:.2f}%, average change {(path[-1] - b_france) / 4:.3f} points a year")
```

One point more interest costs France about 1.1 points of GDP of extra surplus every year, because its debt is larger than its GDP. A rise in the interest rate makes the EU rule much harder to meet.

</details>

**Problem 9 (Intermediate): Growth or austerity?** A hypothetical country pays an interest rate of 4 percent on its debt, its nominal GDP grows by 3 percent a year, and its primary budget is balanced. Its government can choose one of two reforms, each kept for 20 years:

- **Plan A (austerity):** a primary surplus of 1 percent of GDP every year ($d = -1$), with growth unchanged;
- **Plan B (growth):** reforms that raise nominal growth to 4 percent a year, with a balanced primary budget ($d = 0$).

(a) The debt starts at 100 percent of GDP. Which plan leaves the lower debt ratio after 20 years?

(b) Repeat for a starting ratio of 50 percent and of 150 percent of GDP.

(c) Find the starting ratio at which the two plans tie. Explain the result with equation (6), and use equation (8) to show why the tie is exact.

<details><summary>Hint</summary>

Plan A is `g = 3`, `d = -1`; Plan B is `g = 4`, `d = 0`. Compare the two "after 20 years" numbers in the title. For (c), compare what each plan subtracts from the change in the ratio in the first year, using equation (6): one of the two effects grows with the debt, the other does not.

</details>

```{python}
#| kind: widget
def growth_or_austerity(b0=100.0, g=3.0, d=0.0):
    """Equation (5) for 20 years with i = 4%: the debt ratio with growth g and a constant primary deficit d."""
    path = [b0] + debt_ratio_path(b0, 0.04, g / 100, [d] * 20)
    no_reform = [b0] + debt_ratio_path(b0, 0.04, 0.03, [0.0] * 20)
    end = round(path[-1], 1) + 0.0               # + 0.0 prints a tiny negative number as 0.0, not -0.0
    low, high = 0, 150
    if b0 > 100:
        high = 300                               # a second, fixed scale for high debts
    if min(path) < 10:
        low = -50                                # room below zero: the government may end up owning more than it owes
    fig = go.Figure()
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=list(range(21)), y=no_reform, mode="lines", name="No reform (g = 3%, d = 0)",
                             line=dict(color=GRAY, width=2, dash="dash")))
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=list(range(21)), y=path, mode="lines", name="This plan",
                             line=dict(color=BLUE, width=3)))
    fig.update_layout(title=f"After 20 years: {end:.1f}% of GDP (no reform: {no_reform[-1]:.1f}%)",
                      xaxis=dict(title="Years from now", range=[0, 20]),
                      yaxis=dict(title="Debt (% of GDP)", range=[low, high]),
                      legend=dict(x=0.01, y=0.99, xanchor="left", yanchor="top"))
    return fig


interact(growth_or_austerity,
         b0=FloatSlider(value=100.0, min=20.0, max=200.0, step=1.0, description="starting debt b0", style=WIDE),
         g=FloatSlider(value=3.0, min=3.0, max=5.0, step=0.5, description="nominal growth g (%)", style=WIDE),
         d=FloatSlider(value=0.0, min=-2.0, max=1.0, step=0.5, description="primary deficit d", style=WIDE));
```

**Source.** A calculator built on the debt-ratio tools of the Model overview, equations (5) to (8), adapted from the discussion of growth and the debt-GDP ratio in Chapter 18 of Jones (2024), [*Macroeconomics*, 6th ed.](https://wwnorton.com/books/9781324063612)

```{python}
# Your answer here
```

**Your answer:**

<!-- cell -->

<details><summary>Solution</summary>

**(a)** Starting from 100 percent, with no reform the ratio rises to 121.3 percent after 20 years. Plan A ends at 99.4 percent and Plan B at 100.0 percent: austerity wins, but only just.

**(b)** From 50 percent, Plan A ends at 38.7 and Plan B at 50.0 percent: austerity wins clearly. From 150 percent, Plan A ends at 160.0 and Plan B at 150.0 percent: now growth wins, and austerity does not even stop the ratio from rising.

```python
for b0 in [50, 100, 103, 150]:
    plan_a = debt_ratio_path(b0, 0.04, 0.03, [-1.0] * 20)[-1]
    plan_b = debt_ratio_path(b0, 0.04, 0.04, [0.0] * 20)[-1]
    print(f"start {b0}%: Plan A {plan_a:.1f}%, Plan B {plan_b:.1f}%")
```

**(c)** The two plans tie at a starting ratio of 103 percent of GDP. By equation (6), Plan A lowers the change in the ratio by 1 point a year, whatever the debt. Plan B removes the interest-minus-growth term $\frac{i-g}{1+g}\,b = \frac{0.01}{1.03}\,b$, which is proportional to the debt: it is worth $0.0097\,b$ points, so more than 1 point when $b > 103$. **Growth works on the whole stock of debt; a surplus is a fixed amount.**

The tie is exact, by equation (8). Under Plan B, $i = g$ and $d = 0$, so the ratio stays at $b_0$. Under Plan A, the steady state is

$$b^* = \frac{1+g}{g-i}\,d = \frac{1.03}{0.03 - 0.04} \times (-1) = 103,$$

and equation (8), $b_{20} = b^* + \left(\frac{1.04}{1.03}\right)^{20}(b_0 - b^*)$, keeps the ratio at $b^*$ when it starts there. Since $i > g$ under Plan A, $b^*$ is the tipping point of the Model overview: below 103 percent the ratio falls further and further below $b^*$, above it the ratio rises without limit. In this example, for highly indebted countries such as Italy (135.3 percent of GDP in 2024 in our data) or Japan, a lasting rise in growth is worth more than a surplus of the same size.

</details>

**Problem 10 (Challenge): Health costs and the debt in 2056.** CBO's projections of Figs. 6 and 7 assume a path for Medicare and Medicaid, which reach 8.1 percent of GDP in FY2056. Health costs are hard to forecast. Suppose the cost per recipient grows by `extra` points a year faster (or slower, if negative) than CBO assumes, from FY2026 on. By equation (11), the health share then grows by `extra` points a year faster too, and the extra spending adds to CBO's primary deficits. The calculator draws the debt ratio (with nominal growth $g = 4\%$) next to CBO's path with $i = g = 4\%$.

(a) With $i = 4\%$, what are health spending and the debt ratio in FY2056 if costs grow 1 point a year faster than CBO assumes? Compare the effect on the debt with that of an interest rate one point above growth ($i = 5\%$) and CBO's health path.

(b) Congress wants the FY2056 debt ratio below 150 percent of GDP ($i = 4\%$). What is the smallest slowdown of health costs, on the slider, that achieves it?

(c) Could cost control alone bring the FY2056 ratio back to its FY2025 level of 99.5 percent? Try the largest slowdown on the slider, and explain what you find with the primary deficits of Fig. 6.

<details><summary>Hint</summary>

Read the title: it shows the FY2056 debt ratio and the health share. For (a), set the extra cost growth to 1, then set it back to 0 and move the interest rate to 5. For (c), compare the health share in FY2056 at the largest slowdown with its FY2025 level in Fig. 7 (6.0 percent of GDP), and remember that CBO projects primary deficits even without any rise in health spending.

</details>

```{python}
#| kind: widget
cbo_health = components[components.projection == 1].medicare_medicaid.tolist()   # FY2026-2056, % of GDP
cbo_path = debt_ratio_path(b_2025, 0.04, 0.04, cbo_deficits)                     # CBO's deficits, i = g = 4%


def health_and_debt(extra=0.0, i=4.0, g=4.0):
    """Equations (11) and (5): the debt ratio when health costs grow `extra` points a year faster than CBO's."""
    deficits = []
    for t in range(len(cbo_deficits)):
        share = cbo_health[t] * (1 + extra / 100) ** (t + 1)        # after the loop: the FY2056 share
        deficits.append(cbo_deficits[t] + share - cbo_health[t])
    path = debt_ratio_path(b_2025, i / 100, g / 100, deficits)
    fig = go.Figure()
    years = [2025] + cbo.year.tolist()           # start the lines at the FY2025 ratio
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=years, y=[b_2025] + cbo_path, mode="lines", name="CBO, i = g = 4%",
                             line=dict(color=GRAY, width=2, dash="dash")))
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=years, y=[b_2025] + path, mode="lines", name="This scenario",
                             line=dict(color=BLUE, width=3)))
    fig.update_layout(title=f"FY2056: debt {path[-1]:.1f}% of GDP, Medicare and Medicaid {share:.1f}% of GDP",
                      xaxis=dict(title="Fiscal year", range=[2025, 2057]),
                      yaxis=dict(title="Debt held by the public (% of GDP)", range=[0, 400],
                                 tickvals=[50, 100, 150, 200, 250, 300, 350, 400]),
                      legend=dict(x=0.01, y=0.99, xanchor="left", yanchor="top"))
    return fig


interact(health_and_debt,
         extra=FloatSlider(value=0.0, min=-2.0, max=2.0, step=0.25, description="extra cost growth", style=WIDE),
         i=FloatSlider(value=4.0, min=3.0, max=6.0, step=0.5, description="interest rate i (%)", style=WIDE),
         g=fixed(4.0));
```

**Source.** The debt projection of Fig. 6 above, with the health spending of Fig. 7 and equation (11), adapted from the discussion of Figs. 18.6 and 18.7 in Jones (2024), [*Macroeconomics*, 6th ed.](https://wwnorton.com/books/9781324063612)

```{python}
# Your answer here
```

**Your answer:**

<!-- cell -->

<details><summary>Solution</summary>

Equation (11) says the health share grows at $g_{N_r/N} + (g_c - g_y)$. Adding `extra` points to $g_c$ multiplies CBO's share in year $t$ after FY2025 by $(1 + \text{extra}/100)^t$. With $i = g$, equation (5) simply adds up the primary deficits, so every extra point of health spending stays in the debt ratio.

```python
for extra, i in [(0.0, 4.0), (1.0, 4.0), (0.0, 5.0), (-0.25, 4.0), (-0.5, 4.0), (-2.0, 4.0)]:
    fig = health_and_debt(extra, i)
    print(f"extra {extra:+.2f}, i = {i}%:", fig.layout.title.text)
debt_cbo = health_and_debt(0.0, 4.0).data[1].y[-1]     # the FY2056 end of the blue line, unrounded
print(f"Extra FY2056 debt: health costs +1 point {health_and_debt(1.0, 4.0).data[1].y[-1] - debt_cbo:.1f}, "
      f"i = 5% {health_and_debt(0.0, 5.0).data[1].y[-1] - debt_cbo:.1f} points of GDP")
```

**(a)** With CBO's path and $i = 4\%$, the FY2056 ratio is 164.2 percent of GDP, with health spending at 8.1 percent. If costs grow 1 point a year faster, health spending reaches 11.0 percent of GDP in FY2056 ($8.085 \times 1.01^{31}$) and the debt 205.3 percent: 41.1 points more. An interest rate one point above growth, with CBO's health path, gives 208.8 percent, 44.7 points more. (The last line of the code subtracts the unrounded ratios, so a gap can differ by 0.1 from the difference of the rounded titles.) **One point of extra health-cost growth weighs about as much as one point of $i - g$**, because both compound year after year.

**(b)** A slowdown of 0.25 point a year leaves the ratio at 155.2 percent; a slowdown of **0.5 point** a year brings it to 146.6 percent, below 150. Health spending is then 6.9 percent of GDP in FY2056 instead of 8.1.

**(c)** No. Even a slowdown of 2 points a year, which pushes health spending down to 4.3 percent of GDP in FY2056, below its FY2025 level of 6.0 percent, leaves the debt at 103.4 percent of GDP, after a peak of 116.5 percent. Cost control works slowly: the slowdown saves only 0.12 point of GDP in FY2026 and builds up year after year, while CBO's primary deficits, about 2 percent of GDP a year (Fig. 6), start right away. Health is the part of the budget that grows, but closing the gap quickly also needs higher revenue or lower spending elsewhere, the two "possible solutions" of the chapter.

</details>
